about: Single ingredients rated per typical serving, using nutrient values from USDA FoodData Central (often via NIH Office of Dietary Supplements tables), polyphenol totals from Phenol-Explorer and FDA/EPA fish-mercury categories. The rules are in research/FOOD-RUBRIC.md. A score is how much of each evidence-backed component a serving provides, not a trial result, and a dash means the category doesn't apply.

categories.name: Plant polyphenols
categories.how: Total polyphenols per serving (Phenol-Explorer), plus carotenoids, lycopene, nitrate greens and whether it counts as a fruit or vegetable serving.

categories.name: Hormetic compounds (Nrf2)
categories.how: An anchored scale: broccoli sprouts 10, watercress and mustard seed 9, raw broccoli 8, other crucifers 6–7, garlic 5, onions and turmeric 4, everything else 1. These plant compounds work as mild stressors that switch on the body's own antioxidant and repair enzymes (Nrf2).

categories.name: Fat quality
categories.how: EPA+DHA, ALA, monounsaturated fat and EVOO phenolics; points off for saturated fat, processed meat and trans fat. A dash means it isn't a fat source.

categories.name: Blood sugar & fibre
categories.how: Fibre per serving, the kind of carbohydrate (legume and whole grain best, juice and sugar worst) and glycemic load. A dash means under 3 g carbohydrate.

categories.name: Sperm support
categories.how: Omega-3 from fish, nuts, lycopene, zinc, selenium, folate and vitamin C; points off for processed meat, sugary drinks and alcohol.

categories.name: Egg & pregnancy support
categories.how: Folate, DHA from low-mercury fish, iron, choline, iodine, B12 and 'profertility' food types; points off for high-mercury fish, alcohol, liver and lots of caffeine.

foods.name: Broccoli
foods.serving: 1 cup chopped, raw or lightly steamed (91 g)
foods.highlight: A top everyday Nrf2 food when eaten raw or barely steamed; boiling throws most of the sulforaphane away.

plants.why: Polyphenols ≈ 41.2 mg/serving (Phenol-Explorer chromatography sum 45.3 mg/100 g) (3); no pigment or nitrate bonus (β-carotene 0.3 mg, lutein + zeaxanthin 1.3 mg, lycopene 0.0 mg) (0); counted veg serving ≥ 80 g (+1) = 4

nrf2.why: Anchor 8: raw or lightly steamed broccoli, glucoraphanin plus active myrosinase [broccoli-mature] = 8

fats.why: Under 3 g fat (0.3 g) and under 100 mg EPA + DHA per serving, no penalty.

glycemic.why: Fibre 2.4 g (2); non-starchy vegetable (+3); available carbohydrate 3.7 g, so GL ≤ 10 even at GI 100 (+2) = 7

sperm.why: Base 1; zinc 0.4 mg (0); selenium 2.3 µg (0); folate 57.3 µg DFE (0); vitamin C 81.2 mg (+1) = 2

egg.why: Base 1; folate 57.3 µg DFE (+1); iron 0.7 mg (0); choline 17.0 mg (0) = 2

foods.best_prep: Raw, or steamed ≤ 4 min, chewed well; chop and rest 30–40 min before light cooking. If boiled or roasted, add ½ tsp brown mustard powder afterwards [mustard-seed-myrosinase] [broccoli-mature].
watch_outs: Moderate vitamin K: keep intake steady on warfarin.
Can cause gas or bloating in large raw portions.

foods.name: Broccoli sprouts
foods.highlight: The richest food source of sulforaphane by far; the catch is raw-sprout food safety, so skip them raw in pregnancy.

plants.why: Polyphenols ≈ 16.0 mg/serving (no Phenol-Explorer entry; estimated at ≈ 40 mg/100 g from mature broccoli chromatography) (2); no pigment or nitrate bonus (β-carotene 0.0 mg, lutein + zeaxanthin 0.0 mg, lycopene 0.0 mg) (0); serving under 80 g (0) = 2

nrf2.why: Anchor 10: broccoli sprouts, 10–100× the glucoraphanin of mature broccoli [broccoli-sprouts] = 10

fats.why: Under 3 g fat (0.3 g) and under 100 mg EPA + DHA per serving, no penalty.

glycemic.why: Under 3 g carbohydrate per serving (1.6 g).

sperm.why: Base 1; zinc 0.2 mg (0); selenium 0.5 µg (0); folate not in FDC (0); vitamin C not in FDC (0) = 1

egg.why: Base 1; folate not in FDC (0); iron 0.3 mg (0); choline not in FDC (0) = 1

foods.best_prep: Eat raw and chew thoroughly (chewing roughly doubles sulforaphane uptake); add to salads or sandwiches rather than hot dishes. Brief warming to about 60 °C before crushing can raise yield, but above 70 °C the enzyme is lost [broccoli-sprouts].
watch_outs: Raw sprouts are a known Salmonella and E. coli risk: avoid raw in pregnancy, for young children, older adults and the immunocompromised.
Not in FDC SR Legacy or Foundation: all nutrient values are estimates (≈); folate and vitamin C were left unknown.

foods.name: Kale
foods.highlight: A dense source of lutein and vitamin K with a solid crucifer Nrf2 dose; boiling cuts its vitamin C and sulforaphane.

plants.why: Polyphenols ≈ 40.6 mg/serving (Phenol-Explorer has no chromatography total; aglycones after hydrolysis 34.4 mg/100 g raw, applied to the cooked weight (cooked and raw kale have similar water content)) (3); lutein + zeaxanthin 5.9 mg (+1); counted veg serving ≥ 80 g (+1) = 5

nrf2.why: Anchor 7: kale, raw or lightly cooked, glucosinolates including glucoraphanin [cruciferous-other] = 7

fats.why: Under 3 g fat (1.4 g) and under 100 mg EPA + DHA per serving, no penalty.

glycemic.why: Fibre 4.7 g (3); non-starchy vegetable (+3); available carbohydrate 1.5 g, so GL ≤ 10 even at GI 100 (+2) = 8

sperm.why: Base 1; zinc 0.3 mg (0); selenium 1.1 µg (0); folate 76.7 µg DFE (0); vitamin C 21.0 mg (0) = 1

egg.why: Base 1; folate 76.7 µg DFE (+1); iron 1.0 mg (0); choline 0.5 mg (0) = 2

foods.best_prep: Massage raw with lemon and oil, or steam or sauté briefly; a little fat helps carotenoid absorption [carrots-carotenoids]. For long-cooked kale add mustard powder at the end [mustard-seed-myrosinase].
watch_outs: Very high in vitamin K: keep intake steady if you take warfarin.
Large daily raw amounts with low iodine intake can strain the thyroid (goitrogens); cooking reduces this.

foods.highlight: A low-calorie fermented cabbage side with live cultures, folate and some crucifer breakdown products; it is salty and often contains fish sauce.

plants.why: No Phenol-Explorer entry; napa cabbage and chilli contribute very little by chromatography, estimated under 5 mg (1); 75 g is below the 80 g counted-serving size (0) = 1

nrf2.why: Anchor for napa cabbage and radish is 6–7, but fermentation breaks glucosinolates down mainly to nitriles, ascorbigen and indoles rather than sulforaphane-type isothiocyanates [indole-3-carbinol-dim]; garlic adds allyl sulfides; scored 5 by judgement = 5

fats.why: Under 3 g fat per serving (0.4 g).

glycemic.why: Under 3 g carbohydrate per serving (1.8 g).

sperm.why: Base 1; no omega-3, nut, lycopene, zinc, selenium, folate or vitamin C threshold met = 1

egg.why: Base 1; folate ≈39 µg (below 50 µg), iron ≈1.9 mg, no other threshold met = 1

foods.best_prep: Eat it cold as a side (cooking kills the lactobacilli); choose lower-salt versions, and add raw garlic or a pinch of mustard powder if you want more active sulfur compounds [mustard-seed-myrosinase].
watch_outs: Salty (≈370 mg sodium per ½ cup).
Often made with fish sauce or salted shrimp: not vegan, and a shellfish/fish allergen.
Very high intake of salted fermented vegetables is linked to stomach cancer in Korean and Chinese cohorts.
FDC lists vitamin C as 0 for kimchi; real values vary, so it is shown as unknown.

foods.name: Sauerkraut
foods.highlight: Fermented cabbage with fibre, vitamin C and glucosinolate breakdown products; unpasteurised, refrigerated kraut keeps live cultures, and all kraut is salty.

plants.why: Phenol-Explorer chromatography ≈0.4 mg/100 g (Folin 67 mg/100 g, which overstates) → under 1 mg (1); 71 g is below the 80 g counted-serving size (0) = 1

nrf2.why: Cabbage anchor is 7, but fermentation converts glucosinolates mainly to nitriles, ascorbigen and indoles rather than sulforaphane-type isothiocyanates [indole-3-carbinol-dim]; scored 5 by judgement = 5

fats.why: Under 3 g fat per serving (0.1 g).

glycemic.why: Carbs 3.04 g: fibre 2.1 g (+2); non-starchy vegetable (+3); GL ≈1 (+2) = 7

sperm.why: Base 1; vitamin C ≈10 mg (below 50 mg), folate ≈17 µg, no other threshold met = 1

egg.why: Base 1; folate ≈17 µg, iron ≈1 mg, no threshold met = 1

foods.best_prep: Buy refrigerated, unpasteurised sauerkraut (or make it) and eat it cold; heating or canning kills the cultures. Add a forkful to sandwiches, grain bowls and salads.
watch_outs: Salty (≈470 mg sodium per ½ cup).
Tyramine and histamine: avoid large amounts with MAOI drugs or histamine intolerance.
Moderate vitamin K: keep intake steady on warfarin.

foods.name: Nutritional yeast (fortified)
foods.highlight: A cheesy seasoning that, when fortified, is a reliable vegan B12 source; check the label, because fortification varies a lot by brand.

plants.why: A fungus with no meaningful polyphenols; non-plant foods score 1 = 1

nrf2.why: Not an Nrf2 food = 1

fats.why: Under 3 g fat per serving (0.5 g).

glycemic.why: Carbs ≈4.7 g: fibre ≈2.8 g (+2, mostly β-glucan and mannan); yeast isn't a listed carb type (0); GL ≈1 (+2) = 4

sperm.why: Base 1; fortified folic acid ≈420 µg per ¼ cup (+1, check label); zinc and selenium vary by brand and aren't counted = 2

egg.why: Base 1; fortified B12 ≈22 µg (+1); folate is fortification, which the rubric ignores (0) = 2

foods.best_prep: Sprinkle it on popcorn, pasta, beans, tofu scrambles or roast vegetables as a cheesy, salt-saving seasoning; for vegans it's a practical daily B12 source alongside a supplement [vitamin-b12-folate-status].
watch_outs: Unfortified brands contain little or no B12; values here are from a fortified US brand (FDC branded data; ODS gives 8.3–24 µg B12 per ¼ cup across brands).
Some brands add 5–10 mg vitamin B6 per serving; with a B-complex this can exceed the EU upper limit (12 mg a day), and long-term high B6 can cause neuropathy.
Purine-rich: may aggravate gout.

foods.name: Honey
foods.highlight: Still added sugar despite trace phenolics; use small amounts, and never give it to babies under one year.

plants.why: Sugars score 1 under the rubric (darker honeys carry a few mg of phenolics) = 1

nrf2.why: Not an Nrf2 food = 1

fats.why: No fat.

glycemic.why: Carbs 17.3 g: fibre 0 (0); honey (−3); GL ≈11 (GI ≈61) (+1) → −2, floor 1 = 1

sperm.why: Base 1; 17 g sugar is below the 25 g penalty; no thresholds met = 1

egg.why: Base 1; no folate, DHA, iron, choline, iodine or B12 threshold met; not a profertility food type = 1

foods.best_prep: Use a teaspoon at a time to finish yogurt, tea or dressings rather than as a bulk sweetener; darker honeys (buckwheat) carry more phenolics.
watch_outs: Never give honey to infants under 12 months (infant botulism).
[refined-sugar-high-glycemic] Counts as added sugar; aim for under 25 g a day.
Raw and pasteurised honey are both fine for pregnant adults.

foods.name: Iodized table salt
foods.highlight: The cheapest iodine source for pregnancy, at about 78 µg per quarter teaspoon; most sea, kosher and specialty salts and processed foods are not iodized.

plants.why: Not a plant food = 1

nrf2.why: Not an Nrf2 food = 1

fats.why: No fat.

glycemic.why: Under 3 g carbohydrate per serving (0 g).

sperm.why: Base 1; no omega-3, nut, lycopene, zinc, selenium, folate or vitamin C threshold met = 1

egg.why: Base 1; iodine ≈78 µg (+1) = 2

foods.best_prep: If you salt food at home, make it iodized salt; restaurant and packaged foods almost never use it. In pregnancy and breastfeeding a prenatal with 150 µg iodine is still advised [iodine-status].
watch_outs: ≈580 mg sodium per ¼ tsp; keep total sodium under about 2,300 mg a day.
Sea salt, kosher salt and Himalayan salt are usually not iodized.
